title: Per-customer queue-depth SLI and dynamic priority escalation policy
creator: Samira Patel
description: Goal: Define a measurable per-customer SLI based on router queue depth and implement a policy for dynamic priority escalation + graceful shedding when capacity is constrained. Rationale: Conventional endpoint SLIs (latency, availability) hide multi-tenant contention dynamics. High-volume tenants can fill router queues and cause wide tail latency for all tenants. Measuring queue depth per customer lets us: 1) detect tenant-driven contention early, 2) trigger targeted remediation (priority escalation for paid tiers, preemptive shed of noisy tenants), and 3) allocate error-budget impacts more fairly. This ticket covers SLI definition, the error-budget accounting model, circuit breaker thresholds tied to per-customer queue percentiles, and the simulation harness to validate policy effects across bursty workloads.
success_criteria: SLI defined and stored in observability: per-customer queue_depth_p95 and queue_depth_p99 timeseries
SLO declared: per-customer queue_depth_p95 < 6 for 99.9% of minutes over a 30-day rolling window for Production routes (configurable by tier)
Circuit breaker policy implemented in router: three-tier actions (notify, priority-escalate, shed-to-degraded-model) with clearly documented thresholds
Simulator shows <10% increase in p99 latency for top-tier customers after policy rollout and >50% reduction in global tail latency during tenant storms
Runbook + automation: automated remediation runbook that executes priority changes and issues a JIRA/incident when threshold crossed twice in 5 minutes
measurement_spec: Metrics collected from edge-router: per_request.customer_id tag + queue_depth gauge updated on enqueue/dequeue. Compute minute-level p95 and p99 per customer; store in metrics backend with retention 90d. Aggregation rules: if customer_id unknown (anonymous), aggregate into 'anonymous' bucket and exclude from tiered SLOs. For multi-region deployments compute both region-local p95 and global p95 with a priority_decision function that favors local region action first. Use sampling for very high-cardinality customers: sampling ratio adjusted to keep cardinality within retention budget.
error_budget_model: Error budget consumes when per-customer SLO window violates threshold. Budget buckets per customer tier (free, standard, enterprise). On burn above predefined rate, trigger: 1) temporary priority escalation for enterprise tenants (move them into protected queue), 2) progressive throttles for free tier (reject or downgrade), 3) alert to SRE team if enterprise burn persists > 60m. Error budget transfers allowed via explicit approvals (manual or via higher-level policy) and traceable in ledger.
circuit_breaker_policy: Three states: GREEN (normal), YELLOW (congestion), RED (sustained overload). Transitions computed per-customer and per-region. Triggers: queue_depth_p95 > yellow_threshold for 2/3 consecutive minutes => YELLOW. queue_depth_p99 > red_threshold for 1/2 consecutive minutes or sustained error budget burn => RED. Actions: YELLOW => instrument telemetry (tag requests), increase polling frequency for metrics, notify customers via console; RED => for enterprise: priority_escalation (move to protected pool); for standard/free: degrade to cheaper model variant or return 429 with Retry-After. All state transitions logged and emitted to event bus for audit.
load_shedding_actions: Ordered actions with configurable hysteresis: 1) Prefix/KV cache flush avoidance and KV warmup to favor sessions with larger caches; 2) Degrade model variant (e.g., 1.0.quant -> 1.0.q4) for standard tier with quality monitoring enabled; 3) Drop low-priority queued requests with 503/429 and a human-readable reason code; 4) As last resort, blackhole noisy customer for a short cool-down period with token refund logic. Each action must be reversible and associated with an incident playbook.
simulation_plan: Build a discrete-event simulator (queue-sim) that replays traffic traces and synthetically generates tenant storms. Inputs: per-tenant qps distribution, session length distribution, token length distribution, retry/backoff behavior. Output metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, per-customer queue depth percentiles, error-budget burn curves, revenue-weighted regret (impact on enterprise customers). Acceptance condition: simulator demonstrates policy reduces global p99 latency by at least 35% under the tested noisy-tenant scenarios while keeping enterprise regret <5%.
implementation_notes: Router changes: add per-customer enqueue/dequeue instrumentation and fast-path policy evaluator. Control plane: expose an API to bump tenant priority and to apply temporary degrade flags. Observability: dashboard 'Per-tenant Queue Health' (Grafana) and alerting for Yellow->Red transitions. Console: surface a per-customer warning banner when their queue-based SLO is at risk. Backfill: run a 48h shadow policy to collect telemetry before enabling active shedding.
updates: 2025-02-19: Scoping meeting with SRE, Routing, PM. Outcome: prioritize enterprise protections; simulator required before rollout.
2025-02-25: Prototype metrics emitter landed (github.com/redwood-inference/router/pull/742). Basic per-customer queue gauge exists in staging.
2025-02-28: Design review with PM + Security. Decision: do not expose raw customer queue metrics externally; provide aggregate console signals. Security asked for audit trail (implemented).
2025-03-01: Simulator v0 wired to historical trace (s3://redwood-prod-traces/2025/01). Initial runs show noisy-tenant scenarios increase global p99 latency by 2.4x without policy.

2025-03-03: Draft policy implemented behind feature-flag in staging (github.com/redwood-inference/router/pull/781). Seeking reviews from Routing and SRE. Next: run 72h shadow with policy flagged on for telemetry collection.
notes: Trade-offs discussed: fine-grained per-customer SLO provides fairness but increases metric cardinality and storage costs; using sampling and tiered retention helps balance cost.
Fallback decisions: prefer model-degrade over outright rejection for standard tier to preserve developer experience.
Rollout plan: shadow -> canary in low-traffic region -> region-wide -> global with staged thresholds per tier.
